p126.002: The two years when he was fourteen and fifteen were the hardest and most important time in the life of Jesus. He was beginning to sense that he had a divine destiny, but he could not yet communicate well with the Thought Adjuster within his mind. The Urantia Book says that no young person has ever gone through greater trials than Jesus did in passing from childhood to young manhood.
p126.003: After returning from Jerusalem, Jesus spent more and more time with his father, and although his parents did not understand their son, they loved him sincerely. Jesus respected sincere religious people, but he disliked hypocritical leaders. At times he was tempted to become the Messiah the Jews were waiting for, but he did not give in. When the people of Nazareth heard the story of what happened at the temple, they praised Jesus, saying he would become a great man.
p126.005: At fourteen, Jesus was growing into a skilled carpenter who made excellent yokes and worked well with leather and cloth. That summer he often climbed the hill to pray and meditate, and he called to mind the history of Israel connected with the land spread out before him. Joseph set aside money so that Jesus could study in Jerusalem when he turned fifteen.
p126.006: But his parents grew more and more worried about their son’s future. Mary waited countless times for her son to show a miracle, but Jesus never did any such thing. Still, that year Jesus grew up loved by people and by God, and the family’s future looked bright.
p126.008: That September, word came that Joseph, who was working in Sepphoris, had been badly hurt when a derrick fell on him. Mary rushed to him, but Joseph died before she arrived. Now Jesus, just past fourteen, became the head of the family, caring for his mother, his seven younger brothers and sisters, and a baby soon to be born. His plans to study in Jerusalem all disappeared. The Urantia Book says that Jesus “⟦Q 126:2.3⟧sat at no man's feet⟦/Q⟧”, that is, he never received authority to teach truth from any human being.
p126.009: Jesus gladly accepted this responsibility and carried it out faithfully to the end. He judged every institution and custom by asking: What does it do for the human soul? Does it bring God closer to people? Jesus managed money wisely, and on winter evenings the neighbors gathered to listen to him play the harp and tell stories. Even so, the family missed Joseph, who had been a good husband and father, very much.
p126.011: When Jesus was fifteen, his youngest sister Ruth was born. Jesus comforted his mother in place of his father and cared for Ruth more tenderly than anyone. That year Jesus tried to teach his brothers and sisters to pray in their own words, and in the end he wrote down on a board a prayer the family could pray together. This is the prayer later known as “⟦Q 126:3.3⟧The Lord's Prayer⟦/Q⟧”.
p126.012: Jesus was sure that he was not the Messiah the Jews expected, and that he would neither sit on the throne of David nor lead armies. While he wondered what, then, he should call himself, he read the Book of Enoch in the synagogue library and chose the name “⟦Q 126:3.6⟧Son of Man⟦/Q⟧”. That was because he felt the story of one who left heavenly glory behind and came to bring salvation to people was close to the truth. Jesus accepted truth without hesitation, wherever it came from. But many questions, such as whether he was a son of David, how he was related to the Messiah the prophets had spoken of, and how he should deal with his family, the Jewish religion, Rome, and the gentiles, he pondered carefully as he worked at his workbench.
p126.013: Life at home grew harder and harder, and Jesus learned not to reveal all his thoughts. Even his mother worried about her son. On the outside he was an ordinary young man, but inside he longed for a friend who would understand his struggles. Yet his burden was one he had to carry alone.
p126.015: When he turned fifteen, Jesus was allowed to lead the service in the synagogue officially. On his first Sabbath, Jesus chose and read words from prophets such as Isaiah, Amos, and Micah. There were words about binding up the brokenhearted and proclaiming liberty to the captives, and words saying that what God wants is not sacrifices but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God. He also read God’s promise not to fear, because God is with us.
p126.016: The people had never before seen Jesus so solemn and full of authority. That afternoon Jesus climbed the hill with his brother James, and when they came back he wrote the Ten Commandments in Greek on a board, and Martha decorated it beautifully.
p126.018: The family had to live more and more simply. Even working from morning until night, Jesus earned only a little money, and it was hard even to pay the taxes. When the tax collector threatened to take even his harp, Jesus gave his Greek scriptures to the synagogue library so that they would not be taken away. When Herod ruled that the money owed to his father would not be paid, Jesus never trusted Herod again. Since he was too busy to meet the caravan travelers, Jesus sent James to find out the news of the world.
p126.019: Even so, Jesus was not shaken or discouraged. He rented land and tended a vegetable garden with his brothers and sisters, raised cows, sheep, and chickens, and led the family to live by working together. The Urantia Book says that the life of Jesus is a comfort to every disappointed idealist. Like Jesus, who faithfully did the duty in front of him day by day, we too can keep our dreams in hard times by faithfully doing what needs to be done today.
p127.002: As he entered his teenage years, Jesus was the head and only breadwinner of a large family, and the property his father had left was all gone within a few years. At the same time, Jesus realized more and more clearly that he had come to this world to show the heavenly Father to people.
p127.003: The Urantia Book says that probably no young person will ever go through harder conflicts and situations than Jesus did from the age of fifteen to twenty. That is why Jesus became an understanding refuge for troubled and confused young people of every age and every world.
p127.005: At sixteen, Jesus had become a fully grown, energetic, and handsome young man. He had kind yet searching eyes, a trustworthy smile, and a voice that was musical yet full of authority. The sympathetic friend and the authoritative teacher were both beginning to show in him.
p127.006: His family had heard from their mother that Jesus would become the deliverer of the Jewish nation, so they were confused every time Jesus denied that idea. Jesus thought his sisters should learn just as his brothers did, so he started a school at home for his sisters, whom the synagogue school would not accept.
p127.007: At the end of this year, Jesus had almost made up his mind to begin his public work as a teacher of truth only after he had raised his brothers and sisters and seen them married. His mission was so unique that no one on earth could advise him about it, so he talked about it less and less.
p127.009: Around the time he was seventeen, the Zealots, who wanted to start a revolt against Rome, arose and came to Nazareth too. Jesus listened to them carefully but did not join, and because of that many of his friends did not join either. When his mother said that he was breaking his promise to obey his parents, Jesus put his hand on her shoulder and only said, “⟦Q 127:2.3⟧My mother, how could you?⟦/Q⟧”
p127.010: The young people of the village split into two sides, and one rich man offered to support the family if Jesus would become a leader. Jesus explained that caring for his family was his first duty and said that “⟦Q 127:2.8⟧money cannot love⟦/Q⟧”. His brother James also got through the crisis with a speech saying that if they let their brother raise them, the five brothers would later stand up for the nation. But because of this, the people of Nazareth stayed divided in their hearts.
p127.011: That year Jesus made great progress in weaving his divine nature and his human nature together into one. He did this only by his own decisions and with the help of the Thought Adjuster, the same as the one in every person.
p127.013: At eighteen, Jesus took his brother James to Jerusalem for the Passover. In Bethany he led the Passover meal in place of Simon, who had died. When James hoped his brother would speak in the temple discussions, Jesus only answered, “⟦Q 127:3.5⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
p127.014: His cousin John came to visit, and the two had a deep talk and agreed not to meet again until the heavenly Father called them. That December his youngest brother Amos died of a fever. To his mother, sunk in poverty and grief, Jesus gave comfort, saying that sorrow would not help and that her smile would give them strength. Jesus’ practical optimism spread through the whole family and, even in poverty, helped the children build noble characters.
p127.016: Around nineteen, Jesus got along better with his mother, and he had really become a father to his brothers and sisters. Jesus persuaded his mother to teach the children in the positive way, “⟦Q 127:4.2⟧You shall do this—you ought to do that⟦/Q⟧”, instead of the old way of forbidding things. Instead of putting the emphasis on evil by forbidding it, he lifted up the good by urging them to do it. Punishment was hardly ever needed, and when it really was, the older children decided on it together, and the child to be punished agreed to it as well.
p127.017: His brothers and sisters each had different personalities: calm James, faithful Joseph, dreamy Simon, fiery Jude, steady Miriam, dependable Martha, and Ruth, the sunshine of the home. Jesus treated them fairly and warmly and was loved by them all. To pay for Jude’s schooling, Jesus even sold the harp he treasured most.
p127.019: Jesus was poor, but he was a respected young man in Nazareth. Rebecca, the daughter of a wealthy merchant, fell in love with Jesus, and her father also favored the marriage, offering to pay for the family’s living. Jesus was sincerely grateful for their kindness, but he said that no amount of money could take the place of his duty to care for his family. He also explained that a son of destiny should not make a lifelong promise until his destiny was made clear.
p127.020: Rebecca’s father said that Jesus was too noble a man to become his son-in-law. Rebecca was heartbroken, but afterward she turned down every other offer of marriage and waited for Jesus to begin his public work. And later she followed Jesus and even stood near the cross. The Urantia Book says that Jesus, too, was tested in every way just as we are.
p127.022: At twenty, Jesus went to Jerusalem again and met Lazarus, Martha, and Mary in Bethany. When Lazarus worried that they had no Passover lamb, Jesus taught that the heavenly Father wants the truth of love more than such rituals. That day the four of them kept the Passover without a lamb, with only unleavened bread and wine, and Jesus called these “⟦Q 127:6.7⟧the bread of life⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 127:6.7⟧the water of life⟦/Q⟧”. At home, for his family, he kept the Passover according to the law of Moses as before.
p127.023: When his mother asked him about marriage, Jesus answered that everything must await “⟦Q 127:6.8⟧my hour⟦/Q⟧”. During this time Jesus learned how to keep going in the midst of disappointment, how to act fairly in the face of injustice, how to fit high ideals to everyday reality, and how to live the heavenly life while living on earth.
p127.024: In this way Jesus, born as a baby, went through all of childhood and the teenage years and became a grown man who deeply understood human weakness. That is why he is our understanding brother and sympathetic friend. Jesus understands better than anyone the struggles we have now as we go through our teenage years.
p128.002: As a grown man, Jesus still lived the life of an ordinary person. Like other children, he did not get to choose his parents when he was born, and he grew up wrestling with his surroundings. The Urantia Book asks us to remember the two purposes for which Michael came to this world. One was to experience a full human life and so complete the sovereignty of his own universe, and the other was to show people the Universal Father and lead them to him.
p128.004: At twenty-one, Jesus clearly knew his two natures, the divine and the human, yet he had already bound them together into one in a single person, Jesus of Nazareth. He was truly a man of flesh and blood. He worked, grew tired, and slept; he was hungry and thirsty; he went through every emotion and was tested just as we are. Until his baptism he never used any supernatural power.
p128.005: The Urantia Book testifies that between the appearance of the heavenly messenger in Jerusalem when he was thirteen and the events of his baptism, nothing supernatural happened. That is why Jesus can fully understand and help people who are struggling. Later, when people called him by many high titles, Jesus did not refuse them, but once, when he was called Immanuel, he answered, “⟦Q 128:1.11⟧Not I, that is my elder brother.⟦/Q⟧”
p128.006: That year Jesus took his brother Joseph to Jerusalem for the Passover. Joseph asked many things about his mission, but to most of them Jesus only answered, “⟦Q 128:1.15⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
p128.008: Around twenty-two, Jesus was busy helping several of his brothers and sisters, who were entering their teenage years, adjust to their newly awakening minds. His brother Simon went to work with Jacob the stone mason. Jesus went to Sepphoris and for six months learned the blacksmith’s trade while studying the lives and thoughts of the gentiles up close.
p128.009: Before he left, Jesus held a family council, made eighteen-year-old James acting head of the family, and had everyone promise to obey him. Jesus purposely stayed away from home so that James and Joseph could learn how to take responsibility for the family. He was slowly preparing the family to stand without him.
p128.011: At twenty-three, with four of them working, the family was a little better off. Jesus took his brother Simon on a trip through many parts of Palestine to Jerusalem. On the way they met a wealthy merchant from Damascus, who offered to have Jesus join him in his business, but Jesus declined, saying he could not leave his family and go far away.
p128.012: In Jerusalem Jesus talked for four hours with a young man of Greek background named Stephen about the true God and worship. Stephen never forgot those words as long as he lived, and later, while boldly preaching the gospel, he became the first Christian martyr. Saul, who watched his death, later became Paul. Jesus’ family did not understand why he liked so much to spend time with strangers.
p128.014: During the last four months of that year, Jesus stayed at the home of that merchant in Damascus. The merchant offered to found a school of religious philosophy greater than the one in Alexandria and to make Jesus its head. The Urantia Book says this was one of the greatest temptations Jesus met while living as a purely human being. But Jesus knew that his mission must not be tied to any institution or group of people, and he refused.
p128.015: Jesus purposely kept the various events of his life separate so that people could not link them all together. He was concerned that people might make a religion that worshiped the teacher rather than following the truth. Jesus wanted people to believe because their hearts responded to the truth of his teaching.
p128.017: Twenty-four was the first year that Jesus was a little free from family responsibilities. Jewish leaders from Alexandria came and begged him to become a religious teacher in their city, but Jesus declined, saying, “⟦Q 128:5.4⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧” He also refused the money they offered him, saying that the house of Joseph had never received charity.
p128.018: The next six months were the quietest time in Jesus’ life, and he communed deeply with the heavenly Father. At the end of the year, when James and Miriam each confided that there was someone they wanted to marry, Jesus promised to give his blessing as soon as they were ready to take care of the family.
p128.020: At twenty-five, Jesus was an outstanding man in both body and mind, and the family had paid off all its debts. Jesus took his youngest brother Jude to Jerusalem for the Passover, but Jude was thrown into jail after confronting a Roman soldier who had said something rude to a Jewish girl. Jesus stayed in jail with his brother for two days and calmly pleaded his case before the judge, and his brother was set free. Jude never forgot his brother’s patience and generosity as long as he lived.
p128.021: That year Jesus set out sand and blocks of wood beside his workshop, and the neighborhood children would beg “⟦Q 128:6.11⟧Uncle Joshua⟦/Q⟧” to tell them a story. Even in the middle of a deep philosophical discussion, Jesus could quickly turn to having fun with the children. The children loved Jesus, and Jesus loved the children.
p128.023: At twenty-six, Jesus strongly sensed that he had great power, but he resolved not to use it before the time came. On the hill he prayed that, whoever he might be, he would always follow the Father’s will. When his older brothers wanted to send away the troublemaking Jude, Jesus advised them to be patient and show the way by their lives so that their brother would choose a better path for himself. In the end Jude settled down as a fisherman in Magdala.
p128.024: In November, James and Miriam had a double wedding. The next day Jesus quietly told James that he would soon be leaving home, handed the workshop over to him, and made him head of the family. Even so, he promised to send money every month until his hour came. The way Jesus set out on his own path only after caring for his family responsibly to the end shows what it means to go after your dreams while still cherishing the people you love.
p129.002: Jesus at last stepped back completely from directly running the household and leading his brothers and sisters in Nazareth. Even so, he sent money to the family until his baptism, and he always cared about the spiritual lives of his brothers and sisters and the happiness of his widowed mother. The Urantia Book says that the more fully we give ourselves to someone, the more we come to love them. Because Jesus had given himself completely to his family, he loved them that deeply, and so leaving home was never easy. His family, too, prepared little by little for the parting over many years.
p129.004: On a rainy morning in January of the year he turned twenty-seven, Jesus quietly left home, saying only that he was going to visit the cities around the Sea of Galilee. In Capernaum he went to see Zebedee, a boatbuilder and a friend of his father, and began working with him. Jesus designed much safer boats using a new method of steaming the boards, and within a few years almost every boat on the lake was being built in Zebedee’s workshop.
p129.005: Jesus lived in Zebedee’s home, fished with his sons James, John, and David, led services in the newly built synagogue in Capernaum, and studied books every evening. Young people felt at ease with Jesus, because he was always interested in what they were doing and seldom gave advice unless asked. The workers in the shop were the first to call Jesus “⟦Q 129:1.11⟧the Master⟦/Q⟧”. After supper the Zebedee family and the young people of the neighborhood would gather for a time of questions and answers with Jesus. Jesus freely shared his thoughts on politics, science, and philosophy, but he spoke with authority only when he talked about the relationship between man and God. His brother Jude also came often to listen to him and became more and more convinced that his brother was truly a great man.
p129.006: That year Jesus came into a new and higher level of communication with the Thought Adjuster in his mind. This was the last year he lived settled in one place; a time of travel and varied experience was drawing near.
p129.008: In the spring when he was twenty-eight, Jesus left Capernaum and asked John to look after his family. John promised to care for Jesus’ family as he would his own, and with Jesus’ money he bought a small house in Capernaum so that its income could help the family. Jesus did not even know that he had become a homeowner.
p129.009: In Jerusalem, guided by Annas, the former high priest, Jesus visited many schools, but he never once asked questions in public. Annas thought Jesus was a great man, but he knew it would be hard for someone without formal education to be accepted as a teacher, and he did not know how to help him. At the Passover the whole Zebedee family came up and spent the feast together. Around the Passover, Jesus met a wealthy traveler from India and his seventeen-year-old son. The man asked Jesus to travel with them to Rome and around the Mediterranean as his interpreter and as tutor to his son. After receiving the family’s living expenses in advance and leaving them with John, Jesus set out on this journey. No one but Zebedee knew about it, and for a time his family even thought Jesus had died.
p129.011: All through his twenty-ninth year, Jesus traveled through the Mediterranean world. During the journey he was known as the scribe of Damascus, or as a Jewish tutor. Jesus never told his family or his apostles about this journey, and his family believed he had been in Alexandria. The Urantia Book explains that Jesus was always careful not to build up a brilliant career that would draw people’s attention.
p129.012: The real purpose of this journey was to know people. Jesus met and loved all kinds of people up close: rich and poor, educated and uneducated, believers and unbelievers. By the end of the journey, Jesus knew almost for certain that he was a Son of God, and the Thought Adjuster was little by little bringing back to his mind memories from before he came to this world.
p129.014: The Urantia Book says that to heavenly beings this Mediterranean journey was the most interesting period of Jesus’ life on earth. That is because at that time Jesus was still one man among others: the carpenter of Nazareth, the boatbuilder of Capernaum, the scribe of Damascus. He went through every human feeling, from great joy to deep sorrow, and he was at once a man overflowing with humor and a man acquainted with grief. Because he lived through the whole of human life from birth to death, he knows people’s thoughts, feelings, and longings better than anyone.
p129.015: The Urantia Book says that Jesus did not live in order to be a detailed example that everyone must copy exactly. He lived a true human life in his own time, just as he was. That is why we too can live in our own time, just as we are, in the same way and with the same faith as Jesus. Jesus is the new and living way from man to God, from time to eternity.
p129.016: Before he turned thirty, Jesus had lived almost all of the life a human being should live as a pilgrim on earth. He came to reveal God to man, and now he had become a perfected man to present to God. When we too, like Jesus, live faithfully in our own place, trusting God, we walk that same way together with him.
p130.002: At twenty-eight, Jesus traveled through the Roman world for almost two years with Gonod, a merchant from India, and his son Ganid. Leaving Jerusalem, they went by way of Alexandria, Crete, and Carthage to Rome, and then passed through Greece, Asia Minor, and Mesopotamia, until at Charax on the Persian Gulf Jesus said goodbye to the two.
p130.003: During the journey Jesus spent about half of each day teaching Ganid and serving as Gonod’s interpreter. The rest of the time he made close friends with the people he met along the way and helped them. Ganid came to love Jesus deeply, and Gonod asked him many times to come with them to India, but Jesus always declined, saying he had to return to his family.
p130.005: At Joppa Jesus became friends with Gadiah, a young Philistine. While they were walking by the sea, Gadiah asked whether a big fish had really swallowed Jonah, and Jesus, seeing that the story was teaching Gadiah not to run away from duty, answered, “⟦Q 130:1.2⟧we are all Jonahs with lives to live in accordance with the will of God⟦/Q⟧”. He meant that when we run away from duty, we are trapped by the whale of selfishness, but anyone who sincerely seeks God is rescued from it.
p130.006: Gadiah also asked why there is evil if God is good. Jesus explained that God is good because God is love, and that evil is not something God made but the immature choices and mistakes of people who reject the light. Because God has given us the freedom to choose, the possibility of choosing wrongly also arises, but it becomes sin only when we knowingly and deliberately hold on to that wrong.
p130.008: At Caesarea the ship’s large steering paddle broke and their departure was delayed, so Jesus, as a carpenter, helped make a new one. When Anaxand, a young Greek working with him, grumbled that if the gods cared about him, why didn’t they get rid of his cruel foreman, Jesus told him that instead he could be “⟦Q 130:2.4⟧the salt which is to make this brother more agreeable⟦/Q⟧” and lead the man into a better way. Moved, Anaxand passed these words on to the foreman, and the two came to Jesus together to ask for advice.
p130.009: When Ganid asked why he was always seeking out strangers, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 130:2.6⟧no man is a stranger to one who knows God⟦/Q⟧”. When we know God as Father, everyone is our brother or sister. Jesus also explained that a dog can know its master but cannot know God, so it cannot have spiritual experience. The ability to recognize spiritual values and to choose truth is what makes a human being a moral being, a being who can survive forever.
p130.011: As they drew near Alexandria, Ganid was amazed to see the lighthouse of Pharos. Jesus told Ganid that when he went back to India, he too would light the way like this lighthouse for those sitting in darkness, and Ganid promised, “⟦Q 130:3.2⟧I will.⟦/Q⟧”
p130.012: Every day the two went to the greatest library in the world and studied the world’s religions together. With Jesus’ guidance, Ganid collected writings from the many religions that teach one God, and he was amazed that all the great writers recognized the eternal God. When Ganid asked Jesus to teach the professors, Jesus smiled and answered that “⟦Q 130:3.7⟧The true teacher maintains his intellectual integrity by ever remaining a learner.⟦/Q⟧”
p130.014: On the night before they left Alexandria, Jesus explained to Ganid at length what reality, that which truly exists, is. The source of all reality is the infinite God, and even though everything changes, personality is a gift that does not change. Just as you cannot see depth with only one eye, you cannot rightly understand the universe with science alone or with mystical feeling alone.
p130.015: Jesus said that knowledge is what can be proved, and truth is what is experienced. Knowledge belongs to the mind, and truth is an experience of the soul. When the two are in harmony, wisdom is born. He also explained that evil is like a shadow that comes about because we are not yet perfect and have not finished growing. The Urantia Book says that ideas that stop moving and harden always make science, society, and religion fall behind.
p130.017: On the island of Crete they rested and climbed the mountains. When Ganid asked why he did not teach in public, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 130:5.3⟧everything must await the coming of its time⟦/Q⟧”. He meant that just as fruit needs time to ripen, his tomorrow was in the hands of his Father in heaven.
p130.018: Once a drunken man was beating a slave girl in the street. Jesus ran over, pulled the girl away, and held the man off at arm’s length until he wore himself out. Ganid thought the man deserved to be beaten too, but Jesus never struck him. This event later made Ganid hope to change the caste discrimination of India.
p130.019: 6. The Young Man Who Was Afraid
p130.020: On a mountain in Crete, Jesus met a young man sitting alone, sunk in fear and feelings of inferiority. Jesus first asked him the way so that he would open up, and then kindly told him that even without words, his face had been asking for help. And he pointed out that his strong body, his clear mind, and above all the spirit living within him were on his side.
p130.021: Jesus encouraged him, saying, “⟦Q 130:6.4⟧This day, my son, you are to be reborn⟦/Q⟧”. He meant that the young man should end his life of running away in fear and go back to a life of serving people as a son of God. Then troubles would become challenges and disappointments would become strength. This young man, Fortune, later became a leader of the believers in Crete. At Cyrene Jesus cared for a boy named Rufus who had been hurt in a cart accident, and the boy’s father, Simon, was the man who would later carry Jesus’ cross for him.
p130.022: 7. At Carthage—Discourse on Time and Space
p130.023: On the ship to Carthage, Gonod and Ganid discovered that Jesus was a wonderful storyteller. When Ganid asked how to make friends, Jesus answered that you should take a sincere interest in people, learn to love them, and look for chances to do for them what they want.
p130.024: At Carthage he talked about time and space with a Mithraic priest. Time is the flow in which we sense events one after another, and Paradise and God are beyond time and space. The more a person grows spiritually, the more he comes to see events that seemed to come in a single line as one whole, and his ideas about time and space grow wider as well.
p130.025: 8. On the Way to Naples and Rome
p130.026: At Malta, Jesus talked for a long time with Claudus, a young man who had been thinking of taking his own life. He resolved, “⟦Q 130:8.1⟧I will face life like a man⟦/Q⟧”, and later he became a preacher of the gospel. At Syracuse, to Ezra, an innkeeper who was troubled because he could not find God, Jesus said that the very desire to find God was already proof that God had found him.
p130.027: At Messina he encouraged a fruit-selling boy, after feeding the body, to learn how to feed the soul as well. At Naples he and Ganid helped the poor, and at last they headed for Rome along the Appian Way. Just as Jesus poured his heart into each person he met, when we offer sincere care to one friend beside us, that person’s life can change.
p131.002: While they were staying in Alexandria, Ganid hired more than sixty translators to collect what the world's religions teach about God and his relationship to people. The Urantia Book explains that most of these teachings about one God came from the missionaries of Melchizedek. Melchizedek taught about one God at Salem in the days of Abraham, and his disciples tried to carry that teaching to the ends of the earth.
p131.003: Ganid sorted what he gathered into ten topics, and his manuscript was kept in India for hundreds of years after his death. This paper introduces the heart of that manuscript.
p131.005: Apart from Judaism, the teachings of Melchizedek's disciples were best preserved in the teachings of the Cynics. They taught that God is one, that he made heaven and earth, and that he is merciful and present everywhere. One saying goes: “⟦Q 131:1.5⟧We search for the Most High and then find him in our hearts⟦/Q⟧”.
p131.006: They said that a person who knows God sees all people as brothers, and that rich and poor alike are children of one Father. They taught that evil should be overcome with good, and that we should not do to others the evil we would not want done to ourselves.
p131.008: From the Jewish records Jesus and Ganid chose passages that say God is the Creator and that he is merciful and long-suffering. The selection includes the teaching to love God with all your heart, soul, and strength; the song “⟦Q 131:2.7⟧The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want⟦/Q⟧”; and the promise not to be afraid because God is with you.
p131.009: It also teaches us to love our neighbor as ourselves and not to do to others what we ourselves hate. It closes with the promise of forgiveness, that even sins like scarlet can become white as snow, with the Ten Commandments, and with the word that God loves us with an everlasting love.
p131.011: Ganid was amazed that Buddhism had come so very close to being a great and beautiful religion even without a personal God. Still, he found records in it that showed the influence of the Melchizedek missionaries. The Buddhist writings say that faith takes away fear and brings peace to the heart.
p131.012: They say that evil is the fruit of wrong thinking, and that happiness follows pure thinking and right living the way a shadow follows an object. As the saying goes, “⟦Q 131:3.6⟧He is the greatest of warriors who overcomes and subdues himself⟦/Q⟧”. So they teach us to control anger and hate, and to repay evil with good.
p131.014: The later teachings of Hinduism also held much of the doctrine of one God. They say that God is the light of lights, that he is close to every creature, and that he lives within the human soul. A well-known prayer says, “⟦Q 131:4.3⟧From darkness lead us to the light!⟦/Q⟧”
p131.015: They say that God hears prayer and that he is our father, brother, and friend. They teach that knowing God sets the soul free and saves us from lust, anger, and greed, and that while a person's bodily friends cannot go past death, virtue stays with us to the end.
p131.017: Zoroaster had met the descendants of the Melchizedek missionaries in person, so the religion he founded in Persia held more of the Salem teachings than any other except Judaism. It teaches that everything comes from one wise and good God, the Lord of Light.
p131.018: God is the farthest away of all, yet he is the closest of all, because he is within our souls. This religion teaches that if we are sorry for our wrongs and resolve not to do evil again, we will be forgiven, and it asks for mercy with a heart that longs to become like God.
p131.020: The third group in India that kept the teaching of one God was the Suduanists, known today as the Jains. They taught that those who walk the path of righteousness will find a place in heaven. They said that a person's greatest enemy is the self, which shows itself as anger, pride, deceit, and greed, and that the greatest victory is to conquer yourself.
p131.022: The Shinto records of Japan had only just arrived at the library of Alexandria, so Ganid was seeing them for the first time. These records say that the Lord values even the prayer of the poorest person. They also teach that pride, even as small as a single hair, hides the light of salvation like a great cloud, so we should come to him with a clean heart that has no lies in it.
p131.024: The messengers of Melchizedek went all the way to China, and Taoism held more of their teaching than anything else there. Taoism pictures the Supreme as one who existed before heaven and earth, quiet and yet great. He nourishes and protects all things, but he does not force his rule on them.
p131.025: It says that true goodness is like water: it helps all things and flows down to the lowest places. It teaches us to repay injury with kindness and to do good without looking for a reward. It says that God rewards us not for what we do but for what we are.
p131.027: Even Confucianism, which says the least about God, still kept a belief in one God. It says that Heaven makes no mistakes, that it has given people a moral sense, and that benevolence is Heaven's greatest gift. It teaches that when we know we have done wrong, we should confess it and correct it without hesitating, and that we should not do to others what we would not like ourselves.
p131.029: When the long work was done, Ganid wrote down what he had come to believe from Jesus' teaching, and he called it “⟦Q 131:10.1⟧our religion⟦/Q⟧”. The one God is our Father in heaven, and his spirit lives in the soul of every sincere person. We cannot see God, but we can know him, and by living each day according to the Father's will we can show him to others.
p131.030: Ganid declared that he would believe God is not only the Father of all people but also his very own Father. He wrote that the fact that all people are his brothers sometimes feels so great it is almost frightening, but that it is surely true. He could see God in other religions too, but the God Jesus showed him was more beautiful, more lovable, and more personal. Like Ganid, we too can respect the truth found in many teachings while enjoying the happiness of knowing God as our own Father.
p132.002: On their third day in Rome, Jesus, Gonod, and Ganid met the emperor Tiberius. After they left, the emperor pointed to Jesus and said that if he had that man's kingly bearing, he would have been a true emperor. Rome was a city of two million people, and people from every part of the empire lived there together. The main reason Jesus had come on this journey was that he wanted to get to know these many different kinds of people.
p132.003: The most important thing Jesus did during his six months in Rome was meeting the city's religious leaders. He chose thirty-two leaders of the Stoics, the Cynics, and the mystery religions such as Mithraism, and he usually met with them one at a time. Jesus never once attacked their mistakes. Instead he looked for the truth in what they taught and made it shine more brightly, and then that truth pushed out the wrong ideas by itself.
p132.004: Thirty of these people later played an important part in establishing Christianity in Rome. The Urantia Book names three things as the most important reasons Christianity spread so quickly in Europe: choosing Peter as an apostle, the talk with Stephen, and preparing these thirty people ahead of time. But none of them ever knew that the man they called “⟦Q 132:2.1⟧the scribe of Damascus⟦/Q⟧” was Jesus.
p132.006: Jesus talked all night with Angamon, the leader of the Stoics, and taught him that the standard of true values must be found not in material things but in the spiritual world. A scientist is a person who studies the facts of matter, and a scientist who claims that matter is all there is has already started doing philosophy.
p132.007: If material progress keeps going while moral and spiritual growth does not grow along with it, civilization can be put in danger. Jesus said that scientists and religious people should both prove their worth by helping people, and that they should not fight each other.
p132.009: With Mardus, the leader of the Cynics, Jesus talked about good and evil. Jesus said it is lazy to take society's customs, or the religious traditions other people follow, as the standard of goodness just as they are. The true standard is the spiritual values shown by the spirit God has sent into our minds. A person who just follows what others say without thinking is in danger of becoming “⟦Q 132:2.4⟧an intellectual parrot⟦/Q⟧”.
p132.010: Goodness is not so much something we already have as a goal we keep moving toward. If an experience makes us feel beauty more deeply, recognize truth more clearly, and love our neighbors more, it is a good experience. The possibility of choosing evil proves that we are beings who can choose freely, but that does not mean we actually have to do evil to find out.
p132.012: Nabon, the chief priest of the Mithraic religion, tried to win Jesus over to his own religion, but in fact Jesus was preparing him to accept the gospel. Jesus taught that truth cannot be defined in words; it can only be shown in a life. Knowledge comes from science, wisdom from philosophy, and truth from the spiritual experience of religion.
p132.013: Because people are afraid of change, they tend to freeze science and truth in place. But truth cannot become our own without faith. Faith awakens the spark of God within us and makes it a power that will survive forever. Growing spiritually means choosing the good more and more, freely and gladly, on our own.
p132.015: In Rome Jesus personally met more than five hundred people. He mostly asked questions and let the other person talk. He listened all the way through to people weighed down by worries and burdens, then offered suggestions that really helped, and let them know that God was their loving Father.
p132.016: After hearing Jesus, Claudius, a wealthy slave owner, set one hundred and seventeen slaves free the very next day. Jesus told a Greek physician that his patients had not only bodies but also minds and souls. And for a poor man who had been falsely accused, Jesus spoke in court, saying, “⟦Q 132:4.8⟧Justice makes a nation great⟦/Q⟧”, and the man was set free.
p132.018: A rich man asked Jesus what he should do with his wealth. Jesus told him that this advice was for him alone and that he should not force it on other rich men. Then he told him first to look at where his wealth had come from. There were ten kinds: what he had inherited, what he had discovered, what he had gained by trade, what he had gained by unfairly using other people's work, interest, what he had gained by his talents, what had come to him by chance, what had been stolen, what others had entrusted to him, and what he had earned by his own labor.
p132.019: Jesus said that what a man earns honestly is truly his own, but whatever he gained by cheating or exploiting others he should hurry to give back to its rightful owners. Wealth gained by talent or by chance should also be thought of not as his alone, but as something entrusted to him for the sake of others. When it was hard to decide, Jesus advised him to decide in favor of those in need. The rich man promised to start doing just that the next day.
p132.021: One day Jesus and Ganid found a little boy who was lost and crying, and they spent several hours helping him find his mother. Jesus said that most people are like this child: they are not far from safety, yet they spend their lives crying in fear. Those who know God should think of guiding them not as a duty but as a privilege. From then on, all his life long, Ganid looked for lost children and brought them home.
p132.022: The two of them helped the family of a widow whose husband had died in an accident, and they also found a job for her oldest son. When Gonod suggested that Jesus write a book, Jesus answered that his mission was not to write a book but to live a life for all generations.
p132.024: While traveling around Rome, Jesus did not say a single word to one man. When Ganid asked why, Jesus answered that the man was not hungry for truth. You cannot force the knowledge of God on someone who is not looking for God, he said; our job is to live so that the Father shows through our lives.
p132.025: When Gonod asked about the Buddha, Jesus said that the Buddha was a great man, but “⟦Q 132:7.4⟧an orphan prophet⟦/Q⟧” who lost sight of the Father in heaven early on. When Ganid suggested that the two of them start a new religion together, Jesus answered that a religion is not made; it appears in the lives of people who reveal God. The Urantia Book says that at that very moment, without Ganid knowing it, a new and eternal religion was being made with Jesus. When a person becomes a partner with God, great things happen. Our ordinary lives too can become a channel that shows God to others.
p133.002: When Jesus left Rome, he did not say goodbye to anyone. The people who knew him waited for him for a while, and later they formed small groups that remembered his teachings; these groups continued until the first Christian preachers came to Rome. The three travelers walked along the Appian Way and met all kinds of people.
p133.003: On the road, Ganid asked about India's caste system, the system that divides people into ranks from birth. Jesus answered that people differ from one another in many ways, but before God they all stand in the same place. In God's eyes there are only two groups: those who want to do his will and those who do not. Jesus said, “⟦Q 133:0.3⟧God is truly no respecter of persons⟦/Q⟧”, and he told Ganid to make no distinctions at all among brothers who worship together.
p133.005: Near Tarentum a big young man was beating a small boy. Jesus rescued the boy and held the attacker until the little boy could run away. But when Jesus let the bully go, Ganid rushed at him and started hitting him, and Jesus stopped him right away. Ganid asked: if mercy tells us to rescue a weak child, doesn't justice tell us to punish the one who did wrong?
p133.006: Jesus explained that showing mercy is a personal matter, but justice that punishes is the work of society and government. Since people disagree about what punishment is right, it is better to leave it to a group that can fairly look at all the facts. When asked what he would do if someone attacked him, Jesus answered that he would do everything he could to stop the attack and to reason with the attacker, but he would not be the first to punish his brother, and he fully trusted the heavenly Father's protection.
p133.008: On the docks at Tarentum a man was beating his wife. Jesus gently tapped him on the shoulder and asked to speak with him privately, and he kindly asked what had happened to make a strong man beat his wife. Softened by Jesus' kind face, the man was sorry for what he had done and promised never to do it again.
p133.009: Jesus told the man that his wife was an equal partner who shared life with him, and that how lovingly a man cares for his wife and children shows how high he has grown. As they boarded the ship, they looked back and saw the couple, tears in their eyes, holding each other. Gonod, who heard all this, also decided to rebuild his family life when he got back to India.
p133.011: In Corinth, Ganid learned about Jewish family life by watching the home of Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus met with Crispus more than twenty times to teach him a better way of faith. Later, when Paul came there, Crispus and his whole family accepted the gospel.
p133.012: One evening two women who had been making a living in a wrong way because of their hard situation came up to them, and Ganid sharply tried to drive them away. Jesus gently corrected him: “⟦Q 133:3.6⟧Who are we that we should sit in judgment on these women?⟦/Q⟧” We do not know what sorrows and circumstances they have been through, he said, and he asked whether Ganid saw anything evil in their faces. Ganid apologized with tears.
p133.013: Jesus took the two women to the home of his friend Justus to share a meal and asked him to help them begin a new life. Justus' wife, Martha, cared for them warmly. One of them died full of bright hope, and the other worked in Justus' shop and became a lifelong member of the church in Corinth.
p133.015: In Corinth, Jesus spoke to many people, giving each one exactly the words that person needed. He told a Roman centurion that serving God and being loyal to Caesar do not clash. He told a builder to build a spiritual character in his soul the way he builds a building. He told a judge to remember that he too would someday stand before the judgment seat, and so to judge with justice and mercy.
p133.016: To a boy who had run away from home, he said, “⟦Q 133:4.11⟧there are two things you cannot run away from⟦/Q⟧”, namely God and yourself, and he encouraged him to face life bravely. He comforted a prisoner who was about to be executed, telling him that if he was truly sorry, he had no need to fear the judgment of God, who knows his real heart.
p133.018: In Athens, Jesus talked about science with a Greek philosopher. Science can measure how energy behaves, but it cannot tell us what energy is. Science deals with physical things, religion deals with eternal values, and true philosophy tries to connect the two.
p133.019: Jesus gave an interesting example. If one man can shear a sheep in ten minutes, then by arithmetic ten men could shear it in one minute, but in real life they would only get in each other's way. On the other hand, when people work together in harmony, with their hearts united, they produce much more power than simply adding them up. In other words, there are things in life that cannot be counted with numbers alone.
p133.021: In Ephesus a scholar asked Jesus what the soul is. Jesus answered that the soul is the part of a person that reflects on itself, recognizes truth, and perceives spirit. Choosing between right and wrong, knowing God, and wanting to become like him are the marks of the soul.
p133.022: When a person's mind makes its first moral choice, the spirit of God comes, and at that very moment the soul is born. The soul cannot be proved by science, but anyone who lives aware of right and wrong knows by experience that he has a soul. Jesus said, “⟦Q 133:6.5⟧A stagnant soul is a dying soul⟦/Q⟧”, and he taught that the soul grows through moral thinking and spiritual activity.
p133.023: 7. The Sojourn at Cyprus—Discourse on Mind
p133.024: While they were resting in the mountains of Cyprus, Ganid suddenly came down with a severe fever. Jesus nursed him so gently and skillfully that Ganid's father, Gonod, was amazed, and while Ganid was getting better, Jesus told him many things about nature.
p133.025: After that the two of them talked about the human mind. Unlike animals, people are conscious of themselves, and they make thoughts by adding their own interpretation to what their senses tell them. Jesus said that when a mind tries to serve good and evil at the same time, it falls into great conflict. The happiest and most unified mind is one wholly given to doing the will of the Father in heaven. True peace comes not by making easy compromises, but by overcoming evil with the power of good.
p133.027: Antioch was the third largest city in the Roman Empire. As the journey was coming to an end, Jesus was often quiet and lost in thought. Here Ganid went to see an Indian worker who complained so much that he had nearly been fired, and they talked for a long time. Ganid helped him greatly by sharing the proverb “⟦Q 133:8.3⟧Whatsoever your hand finds to do, do that with all your might.⟦/Q⟧” Ganid had already begun to put Jesus' teachings into practice.
p133.029: On the way across the desert, Ganid watched Jesus load the camels and drive one himself, and he exclaimed, “⟦Q 133:9.1⟧Teacher, is there anything that you cannot do?⟦/Q⟧” They visited Ur, the home of Abraham, and Susa, and finally they parted at Charax.
p133.030: With tears Ganid said that the Father in heaven must surely be like Jesus, and that he would never forget him. Jesus stood on the shore and watched the ship sail away. Ganid went back to India, became an influential man, and spread the truths he had learned from Jesus far and wide, but he never knew that the Jesus of Nazareth he later heard about was his own teacher Joshua. Like Ganid, who met a good teacher and learned and grew alongside him, we too make a teaching truly our own when we practice what we learn in our lives.
p134.002: After looking closely at many people and nations on his Mediterranean journey, Jesus made his final decision about the rest of his life. Having seen and experienced many places for himself, he was convinced that Palestine was the best place to carry out and finish his public life. Jesus chose for himself to end his life in the very land where he had been born as a baby, among the Jewish people.
p134.004: When Jesus returned from his travels, he went to see his family. They thought he had been studying in Alexandria all that time, and Jesus did not bother to correct them. His brothers Simon and Jude had put off their weddings because they wanted their oldest brother's blessing, and after Jesus came back they were married together. Now only Ruth, the youngest, was left at home with their mother Mary.
p134.005: Jesus got a small house in Capernaum so that his mother and Ruth could move there. That year the harmony between Jesus' human mind and the Thought Adjuster within him, the spirit sent by God, grew much deeper. Jesus had begun his life as God appearing as a man, and now this was the time of transition in which he was getting ready to complete his life as a man appearing as God.
p134.006: 2. The Caravan Trip to the Caspian
p134.007: Around that time the leader of a caravan passing through Nazareth fell sick. A caravan was a group of merchants who led camels on long journeys. Jesus, who could speak several languages, took the leader's place and traveled for a year as far as the Caspian Sea region. Jesus served the passengers, the camel drivers, and the people along the way, and many who met him became better people.
p134.008: Through this journey Jesus came to understand the peoples of the East better, and people from the far West and people from the far East listened to him in just the same way. Jesus carried out his responsibility of leading the goods and the people safely, faithfully and wisely.
p134.010: On the way to the Caspian, Jesus stopped at a city called Urmia. There was a hall of religious philosophy built by a wealthy merchant named Cymboyton, where teachers from more than thirty religions gathered to teach and discuss together. Any teacher who looked down on another religion or stirred up quarrels had to leave at once.
p134.011: On his way back, Jesus stayed there and gave twenty-four lectures on “⟦Q 134:3.4⟧The Brotherhood of Men⟦/Q⟧”. These were the most organized teachings Jesus gave during his life on earth. The Urantia Book explains that the sections that follow restate this teaching in a form suited to today's world.
p134.013: The Urantia Book says that the human race is one family of brothers because God is the Father of all. The kingdom of heaven is not a material nation but a spiritual relationship between God and people. If all religions recognize that God alone is the spiritual ruler, they can live together in peace.
p134.014: But when one religion claims to be better than others and begins to push its authority, quarrels and persecution follow. Before God all people are spiritually equal, and in the kingdom of heaven there are no ranks or classes. The teachers at Urmia were able to live in peace because they gave up the idea of putting themselves above one another.
p134.016: Next The Urantia Book talks about peace between nations. Human groups have grown from families into clans and tribes, and then into nations and empires. The bigger the groups become, the fewer the small fights, but when big nations come up against each other, even bigger wars can break out.
p134.017: The Urantia Book says that as long as nations insist on their own unlimited power, war will not end, and that true peace will come when a government that represents all mankind is set up. As an example it points to the American states, which stopped fighting one another after they handed part of their power to the federal government. Government exists for the sake of the people; people are not born for the sake of the government.
p134.019: If I want freedom, I must remember that other people want freedom just as much. That is why we need laws and rules that protect the same freedom for everyone. The Urantia Book says, “⟦Q 134:6.1⟧Freedom is the gift of civilization made possible by the enforcement of LAW.⟦/Q⟧” War is not the disease itself but a symptom, and The Urantia Book explains that the real disease is the idea of putting only one's own nation's power first.
p134.020: The Urantia Book says that peace and good will come on earth when religion makes mankind spiritual brothers and a government of all mankind keeps political peace. Sadly, after Cymboyton died, the teachers who came later put their own religions first and showed no tolerance, and in the end the school closed.
p134.022: At thirty-one, Jesus traveled alone through Palestine and Syria. In different places he was called the carpenter of Nazareth, the boatbuilder of Capernaum, the scribe of Damascus, and the teacher of Alexandria. In Antioch he stayed more than two months, learning how people lived, thought, and felt, and for a while he also worked making tents.
p134.023: After that Jesus made his last trip through the middle of the country, from Beersheba in the south to Dan in the north. He also saw Bethlehem, where he was born. Then, following the leading of his Thought Adjuster, he went up Mount Hermon and spent six weeks alone with God.
p134.025: Jesus had a boy named Tiglath leave food for him on the mountain, and he went up alone. He even sent his guardian angel, who was always by his side, to stay with the boy, and relying only on his Thought Adjuster he set out to face his final test. On the mountain Jesus finished the task of fully mastering his own mind as a human being.
p134.026: In the last week Satan and Caligastia, rebels of the universe, appeared and offered him many compromises. The Urantia Book explains that these temptations were not about bread or the top of the temple, but about the sovereignty of the universe. To every proposal Jesus answered only, “⟦Q 134:8.7⟧May the will of my Paradise Father prevail⟦/Q⟧”. On that day Jesus in effect won sovereignty over his universe. Coming down the mountain, he said to the boy, “⟦Q 134:8.10⟧I must return to my Father's business⟦/Q⟧”.
p134.028: Jesus went with John to a feast in Jerusalem. Watching the ceremonies of the Day of Atonement, Jesus felt that they gave a wrong picture of the heavenly Father's love and mercy. He wanted to speak the real truth, but the time had not yet come.
p134.029: Back in Capernaum, Jesus put on his apron, saying, “⟦Q 134:9.6⟧It behooves me to keep busy while I wait for my hour to come⟦/Q⟧”, and he worked building boats with his brother James. He carefully finished the inside of a large boat, a workman who paid close attention to the important parts of his job. When news came that John the Baptist was preaching at the Jordan, Jesus at last laid down his tools and said, “⟦Q 134:9.8⟧My hour has come⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus faithfully did each day's work even with great things ahead of him, and this teaches us that times of waiting are precious too.
p135.002: John the Baptist was born a few months before Jesus, just as the angel Gabriel had promised Elizabeth. The Urantia Book says that apart from Gabriel's visit and his father Zacharias' dream, there was nothing especially supernatural about his birth. John grew up as an ordinary child in a small village near Jerusalem.
p135.003: When he was about six, he and his parents visited Jesus' family in Nazareth, and that was the biggest event of young John's life. His father was a priest and his mother was well educated, and they carefully taught John, their only son. The family lived on a small farm where they raised sheep.
p135.005: At fourteen John took a vow to be a Nazarite for life. A Nazarite was a person dedicated to God who promised not to drink wine, not to cut his hair, and not to touch a dead body. People respected lifelong Nazarites as much as the high priest.
p135.006: At sixteen John read about the ancient prophet Elijah and was deeply moved, and he began to dress like him, in a hairy garment with a leather belt. Tall, with long hair, he was a very striking young man.
p135.008: When John was eighteen, his father Zacharias died. After that John and his mother went to see Jesus, and from Jesus' words and example John decided not to rush, but to go home, take care of his mother, and await the “⟦Q 135:2.2⟧coming of the Father's hour⟦/Q⟧”. Because John refused to take the money that came to a priest's family, they became poor, and at twenty he moved to Hebron and kept sheep in the wilderness of Judea.
p135.010: Keeping sheep in the wilderness gave John plenty of time to think. He looked after an orphan boy named Ezda and lived simply, eating mutton, goat's milk, wild honey, and locusts. He read the book of Daniel a thousand times and took to heart the promise that God would set up a kingdom that would never be destroyed.
p135.011: His mother always said that their distant relative Jesus was the Messiah and that John would be his forerunner, but the passages of Scripture and his parents' stories did not fit together well, and John was confused. Still, his conviction grew that the old age was ending and the kingdom of heaven was coming soon, and his heart burned with the desire to cry out to people, “⟦Q 135:3.4⟧Repent!⟦/Q⟧”
p135.013: When John was twenty-eight, his mother Elizabeth died too. John gave his flocks to the Nazarite brotherhood and fasted and prayed. He thought of Elijah as the prophet he most wanted to follow, and because the book of Malachi promised that Elijah would come again, he hesitated for more than two years without starting to preach. He knew that he himself was not Elijah.
p135.014: John dressed like Elijah and, like Elijah, boldly rebuked people for their sins. He was a man who thought clearly and spoke powerfully. At last John put aside all his doubts and decided that he would be the Messiah's herald, and he left Engedi to begin his short but brilliant career as a preacher.
p135.016: To understand John's message, we need to know the situation of the Jews at that time. They could not understand why they, God's people, had been ruled by other nations for so long. Then teachers appeared who taught that their suffering would soon end and that a kingdom ruled directly by God, the kingdom of heaven, was coming.
p135.017: People pictured that kingdom in many different ways. Some believed a son of David would become king and raise Israel up again; others believed the world would end and a new heaven and a new earth would begin. To them the Messiah was the one who would set up such a new kingdom. People with all these different hopes were drawn to John's call.
p135.019: John began preaching at the ford of the Jordan across from Jericho, the place where the people of Israel had crossed long ago to enter the Promised Land. People believed they had heard the voice of a prophet. John baptized believers in the Jordan “⟦Q 135:6.4⟧for the remission of sins⟦/Q⟧”, and this was the first time anyone had told the Jews themselves to receive a baptism of repentance. In fifteen months he baptized more than one hundred thousand people.
p135.020: When asked who had sent him, John answered that he was “⟦Q 135:6.6⟧the voice of one crying in the wilderness⟦/Q⟧”. He was brave but not tactful, and he scolded the Pharisees who came to be baptized, telling them not to rely on being children of Abraham but to bear fruit worthy of repentance. He taught the rich to feed the poor, the tax collectors to collect no more than was set, and the soldiers not to use violence and to be content with their wages.
p135.022: John preached as he moved north along the Jordan. He did not doubt for a moment that the kingdom of heaven was coming soon, but he was still confused about what the kingdom would be like and what part Jesus would play. When his disciples asked whether he was the Messiah, John answered, “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧There will come after me one who is greater than I⟦/Q⟧”, and said that he was not worthy even to untie his sandal straps, and that this one would baptize with the Holy Spirit.
p135.024: News of John spread all the way to Capernaum. One day while working in the boat shop, Jesus laid down his tools and said, “⟦Q 135:8.3⟧My hour has come⟦/Q⟧”, and he went with his brothers James and Jude to find John. When John recognized Jesus standing in line with those waiting to be baptized, he was amazed and said that he himself ought to be baptized by Jesus. But Jesus said he was doing this to set an example for his brothers and to show that his hour had come.
p135.025: After John baptized Jesus and his two brothers, the four of them heard a voice saying, “⟦Q 135:8.6⟧This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus' face was greatly changed, and without a word he went off into the eastern hills; for forty days no one saw him.
p135.027: During the forty days of waiting for Jesus, John's preaching carried a new confidence. When people from Jerusalem asked whether he was Elijah or the Messiah, John answered plainly, “⟦Q 135:9.4⟧I am not⟦/Q⟧”. Among his disciples arguments broke out over whether the Messiah would be a military leader who would defeat Rome or one who would set up a spiritual kingdom.
p135.028: When Jesus finally came back, John stood on a large rock and cried out, “⟦Q 135:9.7⟧Behold the Son of God, the deliverer of the world!⟦/Q⟧” Jesus ate a meal with John and then left for Galilee. When John asked about his own mission, Jesus said only that the Father would continue to guide him. From that day on the two never met again on earth.
p135.030: After Jesus left, John went south and kept on preaching, but he felt lonely and sad, because the responsibility for the kingdom no longer rested on his shoulders. His preaching gradually turned into a message of mercy for ordinary people, while he rebuked the corrupt leaders even more strongly. When John publicly criticized Herod Antipas for taking another man's wife, Herod, afraid of a rebellion, had John arrested and put in prison.
p135.032: John spent more than a year and a half alone in prison. He was often tempted to doubt: if Jesus was the Messiah, why didn't he rescue him? When his disciples complained that Jesus was doing well but doing nothing for him, John answered, “⟦Q 135:11.2⟧He must increase but I must decrease⟦/Q⟧”. He had been the one who prepared the way, he said, and as the friend of the bridegroom he rejoiced to hear the bridegroom's voice.
p135.033: Jesus loved John deeply, but he knew that John's work on earth was finished and that great things were prepared for him ahead, so he did not interfere in his life. A few days before his death John sent messengers to ask, “⟦Q 135:11.4⟧Are you truly the Messiah⟦/Q⟧”? Jesus sent word that he had not forgotten him and that the good news was being preached to the poor. These words were a great comfort to John.
p135.035: Herod was afraid that if he set John free there might be a rebellion, and that if he killed him the people might rise up, so he simply kept him locked up. But Herod's wife Herodias hated John bitterly. At Herod's birthday feast, Herodias' daughter danced, and the drunken Herod promised to give her anything she asked. As her mother told her, the daughter asked for John's head.
p135.036: Herod was frightened and sad, but because of the oath he had sworn in front of his guests he could not refuse, and that night John lost his life in prison. His disciples took his body, buried it, and told Jesus. To the very end John was faithful to the work given to him, preparing the way. John's humility, lifting another up while making himself small, is a great example for us today as well.
p136.002: Jesus began his public work at the time when John's preaching was drawing the most intense attention and people were eagerly waiting for the Messiah. If John was a zealous and earnest worker, Jesus was a calm and happy worker. John's message was “⟦Q 136:0.2⟧Repent! flee from the wrath to come⟦/Q⟧”, but in Jesus' message the call to repentance was always followed by the gospel, the good news of the joy and liberty of the new kingdom.
p136.004: The Jews called the deliverer they expected by many names, such as “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧servant of the Lord⟦/Q⟧”, “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧son of David⟦/Q⟧”, “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧Son of Man⟦/Q⟧”, and “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧Son of God⟦/Q⟧”. They believed that just as Moses had led their ancestors out of Egypt by miracles, the Messiah would free their nation from Rome by amazing miracles. What they wanted was not the salvation of the whole world but the glory of Israel, so Jesus could not satisfy those expectations.
p136.005: The Urantia Book says there was one thing the Jews never imagined: that man and God could be together in one person. The Creator coming in the form of a creature was revealed for the first time in Jesus.
p136.007: In those days devout Jews were sometimes baptized not only for their own personal sins but for the whole nation. Jesus' baptism, too, was not a baptism of repenting from sin, but a baptism of dedication to doing the will of the heavenly Father. By this time Jesus had fully mastered his own mind and was completely one with the Adjuster within him.
p136.008: The moment John laid his hands on him, the Adjuster who had been dwelling in Jesus left and soon returned as a personalized being. And he said, “⟦Q 136:2.3⟧This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased⟦/Q⟧”. In the water Jesus prayed, “⟦Q 136:2.4⟧Your will be done on earth, even as it is in heaven⟦/Q⟧”. On that day Jesus' purely human life came to an end, and the Son and the Father found each other.
p136.010: After his baptism Jesus withdrew to the hills of Perea for forty days. The Urantia Book makes it clear that he did not go there to fast or to torment himself. Jesus came to do away with the mistaken idea that such things are the way to God. He looked for a quiet place so that he could calmly make plans for his new life.
p136.011: In the hills Jesus met Gabriel, and then the Constellation Father of Edentia appeared and told him that his sovereignty of the universe was already complete. Now Jesus was free to end his life on earth at any time and in any way he wished. The road ahead depended on his choice alone.
p136.013: Jesus decided not to teach at the same time as John, but to wait until John's work was finished. And following the instruction not to leave writings that would last on earth, from then on he wrote only in the sand. The Urantia Book explains that during these forty days Jesus was not being tempted by an evil being; rather, he was making many important decisions for the work ahead.
p136.014: Two paths lay before Jesus: his own way, which seemed best suited to the world's immediate needs, and the Father's way, which would please the heavenly Father. On the third day Jesus decided to go back to the world and live his life to the end, and he promised himself that he would always choose the Father's will. And he kept that promise to the very end.
p136.016: The first decision was what to do about the great hosts of heavenly beings who had come down with him. Jesus decided not to accept their help unless the heavenly Father's will was clearly shown. They were always close by, but Jesus himself laid aside all superhuman help.
p136.017: But the Personalized Adjuster told him of one exception. He could be fully limited with regard to space, but not with regard to time, so if Jesus strongly desired something, time could be shortened and the thing could happen at once. The Urantia Book explains that most of the supernatural events that appeared later in Jesus' life had to do with this shortening of time.
p136.019: The second decision was made in the face of hunger. As the Creator, Jesus could have turned stones into bread, but he chose to find and eat food like any ordinary person. Jesus decided that he could use his special powers for others but never for himself, and he kept this decision until he was mocked on the cross with the words “⟦Q 136:6.5⟧himself he cannot save⟦/Q⟧”.
p136.020: The Jews expected that when the Messiah came, a time of such plenty would arrive that a single grape would make a whole jar of wine. But Jesus was not a Messiah who would multiply bread and wine. The Urantia Book says that selfish satisfaction and pleasures of the senses do not give true happiness, and that the abilities we have been given should be used to develop a higher mind and spirit.
p136.022: The third decision was about how to face danger. Sitting at the edge of a cliff, Jesus knew that if he jumped, angels would catch him. But he decided that as a man he would take careful care of his body, yet would not call for superhuman help even when his life was in danger. A display that ignored the laws of nature would not show the Father; it would treat the laws of the universe lightly.
p136.024: The fourth decision was whether to use miracles to win people's attention and support. Jesus decided not to. Amazing people with miracles would only make them follow on the outside; it would neither show them God nor save them. That is why, even after healing people, he often asked them not to tell anyone.
p136.025: At the Passover, Jesus could have walked through the air from the top of the temple and caught the attention of the whole world in an instant. But he chose the slow but sure way, the ordinary and patient method of building the kingdom of heaven in people's hearts. This was also the path his followers would later have to walk.
p136.027: The fifth decision was how to set up the kingdom of God. The Jews were waiting for a deliverer who would defeat their enemies and rule the world, but Jesus knew that the kingdom of heaven is a spiritual work of overcoming evil in people's hearts. He hated fighting and slaughter, and he wanted to come as a Prince of Peace who would show the God of love.
p136.028: Jesus decided to go back to Galilee and quietly proclaim the kingdom, leaving each day's work to the Father. He decided not to draw people with bread, not to attract them with miracles, and not to make them follow by political power. He knew that because of this, many Jews would not accept him. That is why for a long time Jesus did not let his followers call him the Messiah.
p136.030: On the last day of the forty days, Jesus declared to his Adjuster: “⟦Q 136:10.1⟧And in all other matters, as in these now of decision-record, I pledge you I will be subject to the will of my Father⟦/Q⟧”. Then he came down the mountain, his face shining with the light of spiritual victory. Jesus chose the right path instead of the easy shortcut, and his example makes us think about how we should use the talents and strength we have been given.
p137.002: When the forty days were over, Jesus came down from the mountain and went back to John's group at Pella. That day Jesus took care of a boy who had fallen and hurt himself, and he brought him safely home to his parents.
p137.004: Andrew, one of John's disciples, went along with Jesus to take the boy home. He asked many questions and told Jesus that he wanted to follow him. Jesus accepted him as his first apostle. An apostle means a close companion whom Jesus specially chose. Andrew soon brought his brother Simon. John was sad to lose two of his disciples, but he let them go, saying, “⟦Q 137:1.3⟧This is but the beginning⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus praised Simon's enthusiasm but warned him to be careful with his words, and he changed his name to Peter.
p137.005: James and John had spent many days wandering the hills looking for Jesus, and when they heard that others had been chosen first, they felt hurt. Jesus said, “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧You should learn to search for the secret of the new kingdom in your hearts and not in the hills⟦/Q⟧”, and comforted them by saying that they had been with him in the kingdom from the very beginning. After that the two never again envied Andrew and Simon.
p137.007: On the way to Galilee, Jesus and his group met Philip. When his friends urged him to join them, Philip struggled with the decision and then asked Jesus directly, and Jesus answered, “⟦Q 137:2.5⟧Follow me⟦/Q⟧”. Philip at once ran to his friend Nathaniel and told him they had found the Deliverer. When Nathaniel doubted, saying, “⟦Q 137:2.6⟧Can any such good thing come out of Nazareth?⟦/Q⟧” Philip said, “⟦Q 137:2.6⟧Come and see⟦/Q⟧”.
p137.008: When Jesus saw Nathaniel, he said he was an honest man without deceit, and he called him too. So six men were gathered. Meanwhile some of John's disciples left, saying a carpenter could not possibly be the Deliverer, and they formed a group of their own. Jesus stopped by his old home in Nazareth and erased all the writing of his that was still in the house, and after that he wrote only on sand or dirt.
p137.010: Back in Capernaum, Jesus was as cheerful and relaxed as before. His mother Mary hoped that at last the time had come for her son to be revealed as king before the whole nation. Jesus only smiled, saying he must do the Father's will, and he told them again and again to tell no one about him “⟦Q 137:3.6⟧until the Father's hour shall come⟦/Q⟧”. But people gathered, expecting something wonderful to happen at the wedding in Cana.
p137.012: Nearly a thousand guests, more than four times the number invited, crowded into the wedding at Cana. When Mary asked Jesus when he would reveal himself, Jesus was disappointed and said they must wait for the will of the heavenly Father. But in the middle of the feast the wine ran out, and Mary went to her son again and begged him to help. When Jesus refused, Mary began to cry. Jesus felt sorry for his mother, and he started to say that he would gladly help if it were the Father's will, but then he stopped.
p137.013: Mary told the servants to do whatever her son told them, and soon wine came out of the water jars used for purification ceremonies. The Urantia Book says that the most surprised person of all was Jesus himself. Just as the Adjuster had told him on the mountain, when Jesus wished it in his heart, time was shortened and the thing happened at once. The Urantia Book explains that this was not a miracle that changed the laws of nature; it was simply that time was left out of a process that would usually take months.
p137.014: Everyone believed he was the Messiah, but Jesus' heart was heavy, because he knew they believed in him only because of this amazing event. And he realized that he must always be careful not to let such things happen again just because he was moved by sympathy.
p137.016: The next morning Jesus quietly left Cana with his six apostles and asked them not to talk about the wine. That evening Jesus explained who he was, what his mission was, and how it might end, and the apostles were shocked. Their minds were already set on the kind of Messiah the Jews were expecting. His brother Jude said that even though he did not fully understand his brother, he believed in him.
p137.017: That night Jesus sat by the lake, deep in thought until dawn. He realized that he could not get people to accept him as anything other than the Messiah. Jesus knew that he was not a king like David, but that he fulfilled the deeper prophecies of the ancient prophets, so from then on he did not completely deny that he was the Messiah. He told the apostles to wait until John's work was finished and to go back to their own work.
p137.018: 6. The Events of a Sabbath Day
p137.019: The first time Jesus stood before the people after his baptism was in the synagogue at Capernaum. People packed in, expecting an amazing sign, but after reading from Isaiah, Jesus simply said, “⟦Q 137:6.3⟧Be patient and you shall see the glory of God⟦/Q⟧”.
p137.020: That afternoon, on a boat, Jesus taught the apostles that the kingdom would not come with noise and splendor, but through the great change the Father brings about in people's hearts. He told them they were now his friends and asked them to be ready for hardship as well as joy. Then by the water's edge he prayed that this little group would be united.
p137.022: Four months of waiting followed. Jesus held more than a hundred earnest yet joyful meetings with the apostles. No miracles happened; they worked by day and listened to Jesus' words at night. They came to see that becoming friends with God is actually easy. When Peter wanted to hurry, Jesus would say to him, “⟦Q 137:7.3⟧Be patient, Simon⟦/Q⟧”.
p137.023: Jesus also taught them about the various groups of the time: the Pharisees, the Sadducees, the Essenes, the Zealots, the Herodians, and others. His attitude was “⟦Q 137:7.5⟧We are seeking to win all of them, but we are not of any of them⟦/Q⟧”. Later the apostles remembered these four months as the most precious and helpful of all their time with Jesus. Jesus taught them only as much as they could take in.
p137.025: When he heard that John had been arrested, Jesus once again laid down his tools and said, “⟦Q 137:8.2⟧The Father's hour has come⟦/Q⟧”. Then he preached his first public sermon on the kingdom of God in the synagogue at Capernaum. Jesus proclaimed that the Father's kingdom embraces every worshiping soul, whether Jew or gentile, rich or poor, free or slave. That kingdom is not a kingdom of this world; it is not set up by armies, but is entered by moral decisions and spiritual victories.
p137.026: Jesus said that the kingdom is “⟦Q 137:8.9⟧even now among you⟦/Q⟧”, and that wherever the spirit of God teaches and leads the human soul, there is the kingdom of heaven. Whoever wants to be great must first serve everyone, and the kingdom can be entered only by childlike faith. He declared that if you simply believe that the Father loves you with an infinite love, you are already in the kingdom of God. About a third of those listening believed, but the rest could not accept it. The kingdom Jesus proclaimed is not far away; it is already beginning in our hearts when we believe in God as our Father.
